item.title: SECURITY AFFAIRS AI-CYBERSECURITY NEWSLETTER ROUND 7
item.description:
Security Affairs AI-CYBERSECURITY newsletter includes a collection of the best articles and research on AI in the international landscape

Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing cybersecurity, reshaping both the techniques used by attackers and the tools available to defenders. AI agents can automate tasks, analyze large amounts of data, discover vulnerabilities and accelerate offensive operations. At the same time, AI is creating new capabilities for threat detection, incident analysis and response. Security Affairs’ new newsletter follows this evolution, covering every week the latest threats, attacks, vulnerabilities and developments at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

‘It’s 100 percent a national security threat’: Accenture contractor connected an AI agent to the Pentagon’s secure network, and then sent data to a high-risk website  

Security notice — malicious version of Anthropic.claude-code (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) identified in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace  

UK and Germany to jointly develop military AI in 2027

Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer  

AI policy wonks declare ‘sovereign agents’ a threat to civilization

Progress on provable inference for large language models

The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources     

“Black October” for AI Developer Platforms   

ARTEX Exposed: Mapping the Infrastructure Behind the South Korean Bank Breaches  

A thousand fewer paths to root

Securing Muse: More Than $1 Million in Bug Bounties Paid Out

Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles

WorkOS October 30th, 2026 Data Security Incident  

Covert underperformance on safety research tasks

GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents  

ThisBash Escape: Claude Dispatch Flaw Enables Browser Extensions RCE on the OS  

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

item.title: Don’t Hand Propaganda a Gift: Reading the Brenner Base Tunnel SE Breach Calmly
item.description:
Brenner Base Tunnel SE confirms a breach and Everest claims 812 GB. What we know, what we don’t, and why overblown alarm helps propaganda more than the attackers.

Brenner Base Tunnel (BBT) SE, the company building the Brenner Base Tunnel between Italy and Austria, has confirmed that unauthorized people accessed some of its data. The extortion group Everest claims it took 812 GB of files. Nobody has verified that, and a criminal bragging about file sizes isn’t an audited source.

The timeline is thin. The intrusion reportedly dates to mid-October, Everest’s claim to 17 October, and the Austrian press broke the story on 6 November. On 7 November BBT SE told ANSA that operations are unaffected, the systems involved are isolated, and outside forensic experts and the authorities are on the case.

If real and current, drawings, surveys and site procedures would save an attacker a lot of reconnaissance. Together they could show how the infrastructure fits together, and fraudsters could borrow project names to fool contractors. Those are scenarios, not sightings.

Dates matter too. The tunnel won’t open before 2034, at a projected cost of about €11.7 billion, so older drawings may describe a design that has since changed.

Knowing how a tunnel is built does not mean being able to control it. Sabotage requires access to operational systems and weaknesses that attackers can exploit. So far, there is no evidence that attackers accessed industrial systems or tampered with the tunnel’s control functions. BBT SE has not confirmed any encryption of its systems either. Claims that ransomware could stop the tunnel therefore have no factual support.

Everest is a Russian-speaking cybercriminal group. ZeroFox has also noted that the group tends to exaggerate the amount of data it steals. Speaking Russian and operating within a Russian-speaking cybercrime environment does not prove that the group is directed by the Russian state. In July, the same group demanded CHF 10 million from Stadler Rail after using stolen credentials to access a supplier’s data platform. Production continued despite the incident.

The response should focus on practical security measures. Organizations need to identify which information was exposed, revoke potentially compromised credentials, keep document management systems separate from industrial control networks, and warn suppliers about fraudulent requests. Whether NIS2 applies to a project company that is still under construction depends on its activities and the relevant national legislation.

There is no benefit in creating unnecessary alarm. It only helps the attackers and anyone trying to exploit the incident for an influence campaign. Blaming Moscow without evidence would play directly into propaganda efforts. There are three key questions that need clear answers: which files were actually stolen, how recent and relevant they are, and who might still be able to use them.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Brenner Base Tunnel)

item.title: The BBC has a plan for a Black Sky event, and it runs on FM radio
item.description:
The BBC plans to use emergency FM radio to keep the UK informed during prolonged blackouts, with a self-sufficient studio ready for 72 hours.

If electricity fails across the UK for days, the BBC says it has a plan to keep people informed. David Sillito, the BBC’s media and arts correspondent, explained the strategy in a BBC News report, starting with the 2015 Lancaster floods and ending with a simple lesson: when digital infrastructure fails, FM radio may be the most reliable way to reach the public.

On December 5, 2015, the River Lune flooded Lancaster, cutting electricity to 61,500 people. Roger Kemp, an engineering professor at Lancaster University specializing in safety and electrical systems, was watching television when the power went out. The following day, he described the scene to the BBC as almost resembling a zombie movie, with residents searching for phone reception and queuing at the only working telephone box.

Homes lost heating and lighting, while some water supplies stopped because their pumps depended on electricity. Railway stations, petrol stations and shops closed, cash machines stopped working, and traffic lights failed. Only two communication systems remained operational: copper landlines and FM radio. Local station The Bay continued broadcasting using an emergency generator and a single landline. Kemp’s subsequent report highlighted the irony: a society increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure had relied on technologies dating back decades to receive essential information.

The incident illustrated the risk of a wider catastrophe known as a Black Sky event, in which electricity, water, shops and communications fail simultaneously. At a recent UK resilience summit, discussions focused on maintaining essential services for at least 72 hours. One expression often heard in civil contingency circles, “nine meals from anarchy”, captures the concern that three days without food could turn an emergency into widespread disorder.

“We are nine meals from anarchy” is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.” BBC states.

“In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan.”

The government’s Be Ready campaign warns that severe weather and cyberattacks could disrupt essential services, although it says there is no specific threat to the electricity grid. According to government advice reported by the Express, households should maintain at least three days of food and drinking water and keep a battery-powered FM radio. Sillito also recommends a hand-cranked radio that can generate its own power.

The BBC’s contingency plan revolves around precisely this technology. Around 100 people would operate a dedicated emergency radio studio, equipped with secure communications independent of the internet, alongside enough fuel, water and food to survive at least three days without resupply. Reports published by French outlet Telesatellite and Open magazine on November 7 describe a self-contained studio, generators powering transmission facilities and FM radio as the fallback communication channel.

Only a small number of BBC staff know the complete details. The studio would broadcast pre-prepared government announcements, with scripts already published online. These include practical instructions on daily water consumption and disposing of toilet waste when flushing is impossible.

Additional reporting would come from satellite vehicles and journalists stationed at emergency centres across the UK. Transmission towers, disconnected from the internet, would use diesel generators and storage tanks ranging from 5 to 40,000 litres, providing approximately three days of power. Satellite phones would support communications between teams, with agreed meeting points and procedures if those systems also failed. FM radio remains central because it can reach almost everywhere, even during a major blackout or disruptive cyberattack.

The BBC’s planning assumptions have evolved. An insider told Sillito that the original scenario considered outages lasting five to seven days, while the latest advice from the National Energy System Operator suggests electricity could return within two to three days. The corporation’s contingency arrangements have surfaced before. In October 2022, media reports described leaked draft scripts for a national blackout, including half-hourly Radio 4 updates from an emergency broadcasting centre at an undisclosed rural location.

There is, however, a discrepancy in the Express report, which claims that only around 100 people worldwide know the full details. The BBC says approximately 100 people would operate the emergency studio, while only a small number have access to the complete plan.

Concerns about grid resilience are not new, but the massive blackout affecting Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 renewed attention to the issue. Lord Harris, chair of the National Preparedness Commission, argues that the consequences extend well beyond losing electricity. Water supplies could stop because pumping stations need power, while sewage systems could become blocked when water can no longer circulate. Governments across Europe increasingly advise citizens to maintain emergency supplies, and Harris believes the UK has been slow to prepare its population.

Some initiatives are already underway. ARIA, the government’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency, is investing £70 million in high-altitude aircraft designed to provide at least a week of emergency mobile and internet connectivity over the UK. Programme director Rico Chandra has warned that satellites alone have limitations when terrestrial networks fail.

Harris argues that decades of efficiency-driven decisions have gradually removed essential redundancies. One example is the migration of emergency services from dedicated radio systems to mobile network technology, potentially exposing their communications to the same outages affecting the public. The government maintains that the transition to 4G and 5G provides reliable and resilient communications.

“The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid’s 75-year history.” The Cabinet Office states describing the UK electricity system.

Government efforts to improve resilience predate the current debate. In May 2024, then deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden launched the previous Conservative government’s disaster preparedness initiative.

During his investigation, Sillito also reconsidered the BBC’s isolated transmission infrastructure. What initially appeared outdated became a strength: independence from the internet could help keep broadcasting alive when digital networks collapse.

Yet the UK is preparing to switch off its copper landline network on January 31, 2027, while the future of FM radio is also under review. The government’s position is that copper landlines, although useful during power cuts, have become unreliable and increasingly difficult to maintain.

Kemp is less convinced that the country is moving in the right direction. Asked whether his report had improved national preparedness for a Black Sky event, he argued that the planned landline shutdown showed little consideration for how people would communicate during a prolonged power failure.

Sillito experienced a smaller reminder while preparing his report: a power cut in his own street, leaking torch batteries, missing candles and an emergency radio he could not find. His conclus: “If anything, we’ve gone backwards,” he said. “Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you’ve no longer got power.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, BBC)

item.title: Fake GitHub Security Tools Infect Over 2,000 PCs With Malware (2000)
item.description:
Fake GitHub security tools are spreading malware that disables defenses, steals sensitive data and infects over 2,000 PCs.

Cybersecurity firm Doctor Web has found malware hidden in GitHub projects that look like security tools. The campaign targets blockchain game fans and, more recently, information security professionals. The researchers discovered that more than 2,000 PCs were infected.

“The attackers behind these compromised development projects target blockchain game enthusiasts and (most intriguingly) …information security professionals.” reads the report. “At the time of Doctor Web’s research into this matter, more than 2,000 PCs were infected.”

The campaign started two years ago with Visual Studio projects related to blockchain games, game bots and cheats. The attackers targeted people who used crypto wallets. They hid malicious code in project files, including commands that ran before a project was built and PowerShell commands stored in configuration files. They even provided instructions on how to install Visual Studio and download the projects from GitHub, making it easy for people with limited technical knowledge to use them.

Now the attackers are targeting cybersecurity professionals. Their new GitHub projects claim to offer tools for automated scanning, security testing and log analysis. Doctor Web found one that pretends to analyze and clean results from the Fscan security scanner.

The attackers also hide malicious code in Python and Go files, using large blocks of blank spaces to make it harder to spot. Some of these fake security tools even remove the antivirus software installed on the victim’s computer.

Once a victim opens the project, a PowerShell script runs and contacts the attackers’ servers and legitimate platforms, including YouTube, Telegram, Google Docs, GitCode and Pastebin. An encrypted string it retrieves holds a link to an archive, which unpacks into a folder disguised as a Windows Photos component. Its main program is Microsoft.exe, a modular app built with the Electron framework.

It does most of the damage. The loader collects system information and sends it to a Telegram bot, keeps itself running, raises its privileges, and turns off Windows Defender, UAC, System Restore and shadow copies. It also adds its own Defender exclusions, injects code into legitimate processes, and removes McAfee, ESET and Malwarebytes antivirus products.

Its default mode, called Mode3, stacks several evasion tricks. It fakes its parent process, disables Smart App Control, removes security software hooks from ntdll.dll, makes direct system calls, and patches event tracing and antivirus script scanning in memory. If that fails, Mode2 takes over, adding Defender exclusions and injecting through PowerShell.

Three payloads follow. AsyncRAT, a remote access backdoor, runs as two identical copies on different ports, which probably lets two operators control one device. A clipper swaps crypto wallet addresses in the clipboard while taking screenshots, and a stealer takes browser data, FileZilla, MobaXterm and Total Commander configs, VPN settings, messenger files, game accounts and Discord tokens. Everything is zipped and sent through Telegram, and the malware edits the hosts file to block antivirus vendors’ domains.

The attackers are still developing the malware. Doctor Web found an unfinished component that could install itself as a system service, download Microsoft.exe again if someone deletes it, manage startup and install updates.

“Attackers are constantly updating the Trojans to introduce new features. For example, Doctor Web’s researchers discovered certain unused routines that facilitate downloading and decompressing yet another archive—Lodge.7z.” concludes the report. “It contains an Electron project that hasn’t been completed yet. The executable file’s name is WUDFHost.exe. Its code offers us a glimpse of some of the trojan’s future features.”

Doctor Web advises users to keep their antivirus software up to date and scan every file they download. The researchers warn that attackers are constantly improving the Trojans and adding new features.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Fake GitHub Security Tools)

item.title: CISA and the FBI Warn Of Attacks against Industrial Refrigeration Controllers
item.description:
US agencies warn attackers are going after industrial refrigeration controllers. The fixes are basic, and most start with getting them off the internet.

CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and the Department of Transportation published a joint advisory on attacks against industrial refrigeration controllers and cold chain monitoring systems. The activity is global. Healthcare, chemical, food and transport companies use these systems to watch temperatures, keep logs, run defrost cycles and save energy, including in refrigerated trucks.

“The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.” reads the advisory published by CISA. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

The targets are electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold-storage sites. Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles. In plain terms, someone could cook your freezer from the other side of the world.

The agencies identify three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and exploiting weak configurations. Once inside, an attacker can change temperatures, which can shorten equipment life, create a fire hazard and destroy stock. Spoiled products that reach consumers can also create a safety risk.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.” continues the adviosry.

An attacker can also hide the damage. Operators lose sight of current temperatures, and that’s a bad moment to learn a cold room has been warm for hours.

CISA’s Chris Butera adds that every organization that depends on these systems should assume it’s a target. The advice follows the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals from CISA and NIST, a minimum set of practices for any organization.

Start with exposure. Keep controller panels off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an up-to-date firewall or similar gateway in front of it. Then separate industrial equipment from the office network with its own virtual network.

Next, fix the basics. Change default passwords, use strong ones, and add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where you can. Update firmware, and retire or replace devices the maker no longer supports.

item.title: QNAP Warns Users as Plex2Shell Flaws Are Used to Hack NAS Devices
item.description:
Taiwanese vendor QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server after reports of NAS compromises through the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server through the QNAP App Center after reports that threat actors exploited the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain to compromise NAS devices.

“QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through these vulnerabilities, and QNAP Technical Support is assisting the affected usersadvisory published by QNAP. ” reads the report published by the vendor. “The QNAP Product Security Incident Response Team (QNAP PSIRT) has confirmed that the vulnerabilities exist only in Plex Media Server; QTS, QuTS hero, and other QNAP operating systems are not themselves affected.”

Plex Media Server is designed to make movies, music, and other media available across devices. But when a server is exposed to the internet and runs vulnerable software, it can become an entry point for attackers who have little interest in your film collection.

On October 16, 2026, security researcher Zach Main published technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code for a vulnerability chain dubbed Plex2Shell. Within a day, researchers had observed attackers using the exploit against an internet-facing honeypot, deploying cryptocurrency-mining malware and proxy software. The incident is a reminder of how quickly a public exploit can be weaponized by threat actors.

The chain combines four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. Together, they can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers without valid credentials, provided the required conditions are met. The code runs with the privileges of the Plex service, giving attackers an opportunity to install additional software and abuse the host.

The technical details are available in Main’s original analysis, Plex2Shell. Plex had been notified of the vulnerabilities on July 27 and acknowledged the report on August 4, awarding a bug bounty. The company released fixes in September, before the exploit code became public.

The loader does not check the library’s name, executable permissions, digital signature, or symbols. As a result, the library’s ELF constructor can run with the same privileges as the Plex service.

“It doesn’t check for a lib prefix, doesn’t require the execute bit, doesn’t verify any signature, and doesn’t look for any specific symbol.” reads the report published by zmain.com. “When dlopen loads a shared object, it runs the ELF’s DT_INIT_ARRAY (constructor functions) before doing any symbol resolution. A .so that only has a constructor and no exported symbols will still execute its code on load. We then trigger a second transcode. The codec directory gets re-enumerated, the .so we wrote in Stage 4 gets loaded, and the constructor runs as uid=1000(plex).”

That detail matters because the final stage can exploit how Plex loads shared libraries. The chain uses a setting related to transcoding to influence execution, allowing a specially crafted library to run when Plex loads it. The result can be code execution under the service account, without requiring the attacker to obtain an interactive login first.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server immediately, users should go to App Center, open My Apps and update Plex Media Server to version 1.43.3 or later. They should then check in Plex Web, under Settings and General, that the installed version is 1.43.3.10861 or later. QNAP will release further updates after verifying them, but users should not wait.

If Plex was reachable from the internet while running version 1.43.2 or earlier, users should treat the NAS as potentially compromised. This may apply if Plex Remote Access was enabled, port 32400 was forwarded, or the port was opened automatically through UPnP or router settings. Updating alone will not remove anything an attacker may have installed.

In those cases, users should follow QNAP’s FAQ to perform a clean reinstall, check for signs of compromise and reset both their Plex and NAS credentials. The company also advises disabling Plex Remote Access if it is not needed and avoiding port forwarding for port 32400. Users who need remote access should use a VPN instead.

QNAP also recommends keeping QTS or QuTS hero and all installed apps up to date. Step-by-step instructions are available in the Plex2Shell: Check and Remediation FAQ for QNAP NAS Users.

CISA added Plex2Shell flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 20, 2026, urging federal agencies to addresse them by October 23, 2026.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, QNAP)

item.title: France Blames Iran for the Supermarket Fridge Attacks
item.description:
France blames Iran for supermarket fridge attacks. What’s known, what remains unclear, and how to secure exposed controllers.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the attacks on supermarket fridges in France on 11 and 12 October. He said they hit 700 sites and raised refrigerator temperatures. Some stores threw away their entire stock of perishable food, and fires broke out in several.

“France attributes destabilization and sabotage campaigns against French interests to the Islamic Republic of Iran (electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran – IRGC-ECC).” reads the announcement published by French cybersecurity agency ANSSI. “Following its investigation, C4 is able to attribute these destructive actions to the Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran (IRGC-ECC): infrastructure characteristics, use of signing tools, relay of the attack by a propaganda organ linked to Shahid Kaveh, traces of the use of Persian in the attack infrastructure.”

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot described the attack as “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression” and called it the first major cyber sabotage operation on French soil. He promised EU-level sanctions, and France summoned the Iranian ambassador. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the response should be strong, adding that she had only just learned about France’s attribution.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said of the cyberattacks on French supermarkets, which occurred on October 11 and 12, and reported Le Monde.

“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” said Barrot. “It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people.”

“We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible,” he added.

Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation into the head of Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit tied to the Guards’ Electronic and Cyber Center, and his two deputies. Anyone else they identify can be added to the case.

The attribution cites shared infrastructure, attack tools, Persian-language traces, and amplification by a group-linked propaganda outlet.

French authorities say Iranian cyber operations targeting French interests date back to at least 2020. Previous incidents include a planned attack against Charlie Hebdo, a 2023 breach of its online store attributed to Emennet Pasargad, and a 2024 attempt to hijack digital advertising kiosks to display anti-Israel messages ahead of the Paris Olympics. C4 attributes these operations to the IRGC-linked Shahid Shoostari unit.

France wasn’t alone. On 2 November, supermarkets in at least nine other European countries reported a suspected attack on their freezer systems. Barrot spoke only about the French case, so nothing official yet ties the second wave to Iran.

This is where we need to be careful. When a government names a country as responsible for an attack, that’s a serious accusation. But the reports I’ve read don’t explain the technical evidence behind it. We should treat it as an official claim, not a proven fact, and stick to what we know. Fear and uncertainty can be used to spread distrust, and that risk applies to all sides involved in this story.


The key issue isn’t just identifying the attackers, but understanding whether someone is exploiting these incidents to promote a hybrid warfare narrative. Hacktivist claims may serve propaganda and visibility more than reflect actual responsibility. If French investigations confirm Iran’s role in the October attacks, the pro-Russian groups claiming November’s incidents could face a serious credibility problem. They may have tried to take credit for someone else’s operations. Still, their involvement in some incidents remains possible.

In today’s hybrid warfare, uncertain attribution, strategic ambiguity, and information manipulation make it increasingly difficult to separate real attacks from propaganda.

The method used in supermarket fridge attacks, at least, is documented. On 5 November, CISA, the FBI and other US agencies published a fact sheet on the same kind of activity. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

The agencies list three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting code and weak settings. They also warn that operators can lose sight of the real temperatures, which is a bad thing to discover after the cheese has gone.

The fixes are dull and they work. Keep controllers off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an updated firewall in front of it. Separate industrial devices from the office network, change default passwords, add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, patch firmware and replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Then limit who can change settings with an allowlist of approved devices and IP addresses. Keep tested backups offsite and offline, turn on logging and read the logs. The last control is the cheapest: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iran)

item.title: Iris Ohyama data breach may expose personal information of 7.7 million people
item.description:
Iris Ohyama warns that a cloud data breach may have exposed personal information of 7.7 million customers, including names and passwords.

Japanese household goods manufacturer Iris Ohyama has disclosed that attackers may have accessed personal information belonging to approximately 7.7 million people through an external cloud service used by its online shopping subsidiary, Iris Plaza. The incident highlights a security risk that often receives less attention than attacks against corporate networks: sensitive customer information can be exposed through services operated outside an organization’s own infrastructure.

Iris Plaza discovered a suspicious file in an external cloud service on October 28, 2026. The company immediately shut down its online shopping platform and related systems, launched an investigation and confirmed unauthorized access by a third party. It published an initial notification on October 29, followed by an update on November 5 detailing the potential impact.

In its official incident notice, the company confirmed that information stored in the external cloud environment may have been accessed or obtained by unauthorized parties.

“Iris Plaza Co., Ltd. (Headquarters: Sendai City, Miyagi Prefecture, President: Ryota Iwasaki, hereinafter referred to as “the Company”), a member of the Iris Group, has investigated the unauthorized access incident that occurred on its official online shopping site for Iris Ohyama, “Iris Plaza” (hereinafter referred to as “Iris Plaza”). As a result of the investigation, it has been determined that some personal information may have been leaked.” reads the company’s notice. “Subsequent investigations have confirmed the possibility that data stored on an external cloud service may have been leaked. The total amount of personal information stored was approximately 7.7 million records, and at this time, we have confirmed the possibility that this data may have been viewed or obtained. “

The 7.7 million figure refers to records stored in the affected cloud service, not confirmed stolen data. Potentially affected individuals include 5.8 million current and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Exposed information may include names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, gender, dates of birth and passwords, some of which are encrypted.

“The following personal information may have been leaked at this time:

Not all of the above information about our customers has been leaked. The items affected vary depending on your registration status.” continues the notice. “Some items, including passwords, are encrypted.”

There is one important distinction: credit card information wasn’t stored in the affected cloud service and, according to the company, wasn’t exposed. Iris Plaza also says it hasn’t identified unauthorized access or data leaks involving its stores on other external e-commerce marketplaces. As of November 5, it had received no reports of fraudulent use of the information or financial losses linked to the incident. アイリスオーヤマ株式会社+1

The company reported the incident to Japanese police and the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 29. It also blocked the unauthorized access route, suspended the affected systems and brought in external experts to support the investigation.

The response extended beyond the main shopping platform. Iris Plaza suspended its SIMPLE STYLE website, while another group company, Iris Tech Service, stopped its websites and new applications for home appliance subscriptions and furniture and appliance delivery and installation services. The company says it hasn’t found evidence that these additional services were compromised.

Iris Plaza has also warned customers about possible follow-up scams. Attackers could use the exposed personal information to create convincing phishing emails, SMS messages or phone calls, impersonating the company or other organizations. Fake websites and social media accounts could also appear, attempting to collect login credentials, payment details or other personal information.

The company is asking customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords on other services to change them. It also says it will contact potentially affected individuals individually as the investigation progresses. Customers should be particularly careful with messages claiming to provide information about the incident, account recovery or compensation.

“We will never ask for your password, PIN, authentication code, or any other important information when we contact you.” アイリスオーヤマ株式会社

The incident is another reminder that organizations must extend security controls and monitoring beyond their own infrastructure. Third-party cloud services can hold millions of customer records, and unauthorized access to those environments can create consequences far beyond the service initially compromised.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iris Ohyama)

item.title: Google fixes the eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of (2026)
item.description:
Google patched nine Chrome flaws, including a V8 vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-125350, that attackers have been actively exploiting in the wild.


Google has addressed multiple security vulnerabilities, one of which, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, has been actively exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability is a use after free issue that resides in XML and was reported by an anonymous source on November 6, 2026..

“Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” reads the advisory.

A Use-after-free (UAF) is a memory corruption vulnerability that occurs when a program continues to use a piece of memory after it has been released (freed).

In simple terms, an application allocates memory to store data, then releases that memory when it is no longer needed. A use-after-free bug occurs when the application later tries to access that same memory location, even though it is no longer valid.

Attackers may exploit a use-after-free vulnerability to crash an application and cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code. Depending on the affected component and the nature of the flaw, successful exploitation could also allow attackers to escalate their privileges.

The IT giant has not shared further details about how attackers are exploiting the vulnerability or who is behind the attacks.

“Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix. We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven’t yet fixed.” continues the advisory.

CVE-2026-125350 is the eighth exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026. Since the start of the year, Google has addressed the following zero-day flaws exploited in attacks in the wild:

Google has released Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update will roll out gradually over the coming days and weeks.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Google)

item.title: iOS Sandbox Escape Is Public, and Apple Hasn’t Confirmed a Fix
item.description:
A public iOS sandbox escape could expose wallet keys, Binance warns. No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed.

On 10 November, Binance warned users about a public iOS sandbox escape that lets one app read the files of other apps. Seed phrases, private keys and login credentials could be exposed to a malicious app, the exchange said.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.” reads the warning.

Binance advises users to remove apps installed from untrusted sources, update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions, and, if a breach is suspected, move funds to a new wallet on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

A researcher known as ‘forcequitOS’ published the PoC exploit code, called worse_query, on GitHub. Apple released security updates for both iOS versions the following day, but its release notes mysteriously don’t report a fix for the issue. The good news is that neither Binance nor the researcher has reported any attacks or data theft.

“worse_query is the direct successor to bad_query and essentially replaces it. To use worse_query, you’ll have to set up an App Group container for your app.” forcequitOS wrote.

The proof-of-concept can access the data folders used by all apps and, on iOS 27, some system folders as well. To work, an app must create an App Group container. The researcher says the code is intended for developers and “isn’t useful by itself.” However, other developers have already used it to build apps that can be installed on iPhones.

One example is WQ Files, a file manager developed by Christoph Kolbicz, TheHackerNews reports.

“WQ Files is a file browser, app data manager and cache cleaner for iOS 26 and 27. “WQ” stands for worse_query, the sandbox technique it is built on. It reaches other apps’ and system containers with no jailbreak and no kernel exploit. Tested on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2.” reads the description.

It can access data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak or a kernel exploit. It can also edit, delete and clear that data. Users can install it through sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the required App Group when users sign in with their Apple ID.


The forcequitOS says they have no intention of seeking a bug bounty from Apple and are willing to give up any potential reward because of Apple’s delayed response and the inappropriate behavior of people publicly misusing or exaggerating the exploit.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apple)
